name: The sixteen categories of Nyāya (ṣoḍaśa padārtha)

definitions.definition: The sixteen topics whose true knowledge yields the highest good (NS 1.1.1): the means and objects of knowledge, and the elements of inquiry and debate. The Bhāṣya explains that the latter are listed separately so that Nyāya is not merely a science of the self like the Upaniṣads.

relations.note: Nyāya's sixteen are topics of inquiry; the Vaiśeṣika categories are kinds of reals; NBh 1.1.9 admits the latter as further prameyas.

definitions.definition: Perception, inference, comparison and verbal testimony (NS 1.1.3); tradition, presumption, inclusion and non-apprehension are reduced to them (NS 2.2.1–2). Bhāsarvajña accepts only three (no separate comparison).
The four means organize the Tattvacintāmaṇi's four books.
Perception and inference; verbal knowledge is explained by inference (VS 9.18–19 C); testimony, comparison and presumption are included in inference (Praśastapāda).

Self, body, senses, objects, cognition, mind, activity, faults, rebirth, fruit, pain and liberation (NS 1.1.9) — the objects whose true knowledge liberates and whose false knowledge binds (NBh 1.1.9).

name: The chain from false knowledge to liberation (NS 1.1.2)

definitions.definition: False knowledge → faults (attachment, aversion, delusion) → activity (good and bad acts of body, speech and mind, producing merit and demerit) → birth → pain; this unbroken series is saṃsāra. When knowledge of truth removes false knowledge, each successive link falls away and absolute liberation results (NS 1.1.2; NBh 1.1.2).

Proposition, reason, example, application, conclusion (NS 1.1.32–39): e.g. 'the mountain has fire; because it has smoke; whatever has smoke has fire, like a kitchen; so is this; therefore so'. The members embody all four means of knowledge (NBh 1.1.1); a ten-member view is rejected (NBh 1.1.32).

name: The pseudo-reasons (hetvābhāsa)

definitions.definition: Five in the sūtra: inconclusive, contradictory, prakaraṇasama, sādhyasama, kālātīta (NS 1.2.4–9).
Five in the Navya list: inconclusive (three kinds), contradictory, counterbalanced, unestablished (three kinds), sublated; the adjunct (upādhi) makes a reason unestablished as to pervasion.

notes: The correspondence of the old and new lists (arrows) is the usual later reading, not stated in the sūtra.

definitions.definition: Discussion (vāda) for truth; wrangling (jalpa) using quibbles and futile rejoinders; cavilling (vitaṇḍā) without a counter-thesis (NS 1.2.1–3); the last two are allowed to protect truth like a thorn fence (NS 4.2.50); vāda is held with teachers and fellow-seekers (NS 4.2.48).
Verbal, generalizing and figurative quibbles (NS 1.2.10–17).
Objections resting on mere similarity or dissimilarity (NS 1.2.18), listed in NS 5.1.1.
Listed in NS 5.2.1 and defined in 5.2.2–25.

name: The four kinds of established tenet (siddhānta)

definitions.definition: Common to all systems, peculiar to one system, implied (adhikaraṇa), provisionally accepted (abhyupagama) (NS 1.1.26–31).

name: Enumeration, definition, examination (the method of the śāstra)

definitions.definition: The śāstra proceeds by naming (uddeśa), defining (lakṣaṇa) and examining (parīkṣā) (NBh 1.1.3); book 1 of the sūtra enumerates and defines, books 2–5 examine.

The same object may be known by several means (fire by testimony, inference and perception), though some objects are restricted to one (heaven to scripture); knowledge culminates in perception (NBh 1.1.3).

relations.note: Buddhist logicians restrict each means of knowledge to its own kind of object.

name: The self as a substance with qualities

definitions.definition: An eternal, all-pervading substance distinct from body, senses, mind and cognition; the one who sees and touches the same thing, recognizes, remembers and is born with memories (NS 3.1.1–24, 3.2.40); its qualities (cognition, desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain) are adventitious.

One of the nine substances, all-pervading (VS 7.1.29), known by marks such as breath, eye-movements, life and desire (VS 3.2.4 C), and by the distinctive use of 'I' (VS 3.2.9–13 C); perceived in yoga (VS 9.13).
The substrate of cognition, of two kinds: the Lord and the individual selves (Tarkasaṅgraha).

relations.note: The Buddhist denial of a self, which Nyāya refutes.
Sāṃkhya's puruṣa is pure consciousness; the Nyāya self has consciousness only as an adventitious quality.

definitions.definition: Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, cognition (NS 1.1.10).
Inhalation and exhalation, closing and opening of the eyes, life, movement of the mind, modifications of the other senses, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort (VS 3.2.4 C).
Selves are many because their states are distinct and on the authority of scripture (VS 3.2.15–17 C).
Individual selves are distinct in each body; the Lord is one (Tarkasaṅgraha).

relations.note: Advaita's one self; the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika tradition insists on real, eternal plurality.

name: The mind (manas) as one and atomic

definitions.definition: One per body, atomic; its mark is the non-simultaneity of cognitions; apparent simultaneity is like the firebrand circle, due to its swift movement (NS 1.1.16, 3.2.56–59); cognition belongs to the self, not the mind (NS 3.2.19).
An eternal atomic substance, one in each body because efforts and cognitions are not simultaneous (VS 3.2.1–3, 7.1.30 C); its first motion at creation is caused by adṛṣṭa (VS 5.2.14).

name: Cognition as an adventitious quality of the self

definitions.definition: Cognition (buddhi = jñāna = upalabdhi) is a non-eternal quality of the self produced by the contact of self, mind, sense and object; it is not the self's nature and is absent in liberation (NS 1.1.15, 3.2.1–9; NBh 1.1.22).
The individual self's cognition, desire and effort are non-eternal; the Lord's are eternal (Tarkasaṅgraha).

relations.note: Vedānta's self-luminous consciousness as the self's nature.

name: Deep sleep in Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika

definitions.definition: In dreamless sleep there is no affliction — the analogy for liberation's possibility (NS 4.1.63).
No cognition arises in deep sleep because the mind rests in the channel purītat and lacks contact with the skin-sense, which every cognition requires (commentarial tradition on the Muktāvalī).

notes: The purītat account is confirmed in a local commentary e-text (Subodhinī) but not traced to a root text here.

name: The special qualities of the self (ātma-viśeṣaguṇa)

definitions.definition: Cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit and demerit — eight special qualities of the self alone (Tarkasaṅgraha); memory-impression also resides only in the self; liberation is their cessation (Praśastapāda, as usually summarized).

name: Nyāya arguments for previous and future births

definitions.definition: A newborn's joy, fear and grief presuppose memory of earlier experience; its desire for the breast presupposes the practice of eating in a former life; no one is born free of desire; since the self is eternal, rebirth is established (NS 3.1.18–24, 4.1.10).

name: No fruit without deed, no deed without fruit

definitions.definition: Body and experience arise from the fruits of one's own past acts (NS 3.2.60); accounts that would make one reap what one did not do (akṛtābhyāgama) are rejected (NS 3.2.38, 3.2.72 DCS); even the Lord brings about fruits without annulling what each has done (NBh 4.1.21).

name: Liberation (apavarga) as the end of pain

definitions.definition: Absolute release from pain (NS 1.1.22), reached by removing false knowledge (NS 1.1.2). Mainstream view: the liberated self has neither pleasure nor cognition — there is no proof of an eternal pleasure, and seeking it would bind (NBh 1.1.22); liberation is peace in which all pain is cut off (NBh 1.1.2). Minority view (Bhāsarvajña): the cessation of pain is qualified by the experience of eternal bliss.
A destruction of pain not contemporaneous with any prior absence of pain in the same self (Muktivāda).

relations.note: the same state described through adṛṣṭa and the body

definitions.definition: When adṛṣṭa is absent there is no contact with a body and no new appearance (VS 5.2.20 C); knowledge of the categories arising from dharma brings detachment, no new merit and demerit accrue, and when the old are exhausted the self, without seed, takes no body — a quiescence like fire whose fuel is burnt (Praśastapāda).

name: The twenty-one kinds of pain

definitions.definition: The pain whose absolute cessation is the goal is divided into twenty-one kinds (Vācaspati); later manuals list them as the body, the six senses (with mind), their six objects, the six cognitions, pleasure and pain itself; birth itself is pain (NS 4.1.55).

notes: The number is confirmed in the Tātparyaṭīkā e-text; the member list is recalled from later manuals.

name: The four topics: what is to be abandoned, its cause, abandonment, the means

definitions.definition: Having understood what is to be abandoned, what produces it, its absolute abandonment and the means to that, one attains the highest good (NBh 1.1.1).

relations.note: Structural parallel with the four noble truths and with the Yoga Bhāṣya's fourfold (YBh 2.15); a parallel of form, not of doctrine.

name: Good and bad activity of body, speech and mind

definitions.definition: Bad: injury, theft, forbidden sex (body); lying, harshness, slander, idle talk (speech); malice, coveting, disbelief (mind) — leading to adharma. Good: giving, protecting, serving (body); truthful, beneficial, pleasant speech and recitation; compassion, freedom from craving, faith (mind) — leading to dharma (NBh 1.1.2).

relations.note: Close parallel to the Buddhist ten courses of wholesome and unwholesome action (list of shared vocabulary; no borrowing asserted).

definitions.definition: Attachment, aversion and delusion; delusion is the worst (NS 4.1.3–6); they arise from false knowledge and impel activity (NS 1.1.18; NBh 1.1.2).

name: The yogic means to knowledge of truth in Nyāya

definitions.definition: Knowledge of truth arises from repeated practice of a particular samādhi (NS 4.2.38), which is possible through prior practice despite intruding objects and hunger (4.2.39–41); yoga is to be practised in forests, caves and sandbanks (4.2.42); for liberation one purifies the self by yama and niyama and by yoga and the method of the inner self — austerity, breath-control, withdrawal, meditation, fixation, and repeated contemplation of objects (4.2.46; NBh); with study, reflection and discussion (4.2.47–49).

name: Reasoning about the Lord as worship

definitions.definition: Reasoning about the Lord, being reflection (manana) after hearing, is itself a form of worship (NK 1.3); worship of Him is the path to heaven and liberation (NK 1.2).

relations.note: Nyāya places itself at the stage of manana in the Upaniṣadic triad.

name: The debts (ṛṇa) and the possibility of liberation

definitions.definition: The objection that lifelong Vedic debts, afflictions and duties leave no room for liberation is answered: 'debt' is figurative; the renunciant places the fires within the self; the stages of life allow for liberation (NS 4.1.59–62; NBh).

name: The six (later seven) categories of Vaiśeṣika

definitions.definition: Substance, quality, motion, universal, particularity, inherence (Praśastapāda; Upaskāra VS 1.1.4), to which absence is added as the seventh (Udayana's Lakṣaṇāvalī, Śivāditya, Śrīvallabha); absence was not listed earlier because it is determined through its counterpositive, not because unreal (Kiraṇāvalī). Candramati's treatise counts ten.
Seven categories (Tarkasaṅgraha, Bhāṣāpariccheda); capacity, similarity and number are not additional categories (argued from Udayana's principle of exclusive alternatives).
Accepted as further objects of knowledge besides the twelve (NBh 1.1.9).
Earth, water, fire, air, ākāśa, time, space, self, mind (VS 1.1.4 C); substance is what has motion and qualities and is an inherent cause (VS 1.1.14 C).

Seventeen named in VS 1.1.5 (colour, taste, smell, touch, number, magnitude, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, nearness, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort) and seven more included by 'ca' (heaviness, fluidity, viscidity, impression, merit, demerit, sound) (Praśastapāda).

relations.note: Vaiśeṣika guṇa = quality residing in substance; Sāṃkhya guṇa = constituent of prakṛti. Same word, different concept.

definitions.definition: Throwing upward, throwing downward, contraction, expansion, going (VS 1.1.6).
Prior absence, destruction, absolute absence, mutual absence (Tarkasaṅgraha), foreshadowed in VS 9.1–12.

Earth, water, fire and air consist of eternal, partless, imperceptible atoms of spherical size (VS 4.1.1, 4.1.6–7, 7.1.26 C); at creation, atoms set in motion by adṛṣṭa combine into dyads and so on up to the gross elements (Praśastapāda); the triad (trasareṇu) is the smallest visible thing (later manuals).
Division of wholes ends in atoms, beyond the truṭi; atoms are partless, since ākāśa's 'penetration' does not apply to non-products and the alternative is an infinite regress (NS 4.2.16–25).

Merit and demerit (qualities of selves) that cause motions without visible cause — needle and magnet, ascent of sap, upward flame, the first motion of atoms and minds — and the mind's departure at death and entry at birth; its absence is liberation (VS 5.1.15, 5.2.8, 5.2.14, 5.2.19–20 C); acts done for the unseen (VS 6.2.2).
A supersensible cause of experience must be admitted (NK stabaka 1); the Lord sets the stores of merit and demerit in motion (NBh 4.1.21).

name: Dharma as the source of prosperity and the highest good

definitions.definition: That from which prosperity and the highest good result (VS 1.1.2); the Veda's authority follows from its being 'the statement of that' (VS 1.1.3); merit produced by enjoined acts (Tarkasaṅgraha); common and particular duties (Praśastapāda).

Prosperity from pure food taken with restraint and recitation; taint lies in injury (VS 6.1.8–12, 6.2.6–10 C); the life-stages yield merit according to purity of intention (6.2.3–5); ablution, fasting, celibacy, residence with the teacher, forest-dwelling, sacrifice, giving and observances for the unseen (6.2.2); common duties such as non-injury, truthfulness and non-stealing (Praśastapāda).

name: Cosmic creation and dissolution by Maheśvara's will

definitions.definition: At the end of a Brahmā's lifespan Maheśvara wills dissolution and all products are resolved into atoms; then He wills creation for the selves' experience: through adṛṣṭa motion arises in atoms, dyads and the elements arise in order, Brahmā is born in a cosmic egg and appointed to create beings (Praśastapāda).
Time and space (direction) are single, all-pervading, eternal substances inferred from the notions 'earlier/later, simultaneous, quick' and 'this from here' (VS 2.2.6, 2.2.12 C; Tarkasaṅgraha).

name: Darkness as mere absence of light

definitions.definition: Darkness is not a substance but the absence of light (VS 5.2.21 C).

The one eternal relation between inseparables — part and whole, quality and substance, motion and substrate, universal and individual, particularity and eternal substance — known from the notion 'here' (VS 7.2.29 C; Tarkasaṅgraha).
The endless particularities residing in eternal substances (atoms, selves, minds) that make each distinct from every other (Tarkasaṅgraha); traditionally linked with the name Vaiśeṣika.

name: The six impediments to a universal (jātibādhaka)

definitions.definition: Uniqueness of the individual, equivalence of extension, cross-division, infinite regress, loss of nature, lack of relation (Udayana).

name: The whole (avayavin) as a real new substance

definitions.definition: The whole is a substance over and above its parts, perceived as one, inhering in its parts (NS 2.1.31–37, 4.2.4–17); the notion of the whole is also named as the cause of passion, countered by the notion of parts (NS 4.2.3; NBh).

notes: The same tradition affirms the whole's reality and prescribes attending to parts against lust — different contexts (ontology vs. practice) within Nyāya.

definitions.definition: Pīlupāka: in baking, the pot breaks down to atoms, whose colour changes, and is re-formed.
Piṭharapāka: the colour of the whole pot changes without its dissolution.
Momentum, memory-impression (in the self), elasticity (Tarkasaṅgraha).

name: The body in Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika

definitions.definition: The substrate of movement, senses and experience (NS 1.1.11), earthy (NS 3.1.27), produced by past karma (NS 3.2.60).

Bodies of earth (ours), water (Varuṇa's world), fire (Āditya's world) and air (Vāyu's world); some beings are not womb-born (VS 4.2.9 C; Tarkasaṅgraha); breath is air moving in the body, one but named prāṇa, apāna etc. by adjuncts.

notes: Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika has no subtle-body (liṅga-śarīra) or cakra anatomy in its root texts; the transmigrating mind is atomic.

name: The senses as made of the elements

definitions.definition: Smell, taste, sight, touch and hearing arise from earth, water, fire, air and ākāśa, and grasp those elements' qualities (NS 1.1.12–14).
Each sense is a product of its element with a bodily seat (Tarkasaṅgraha).

name: Sound as a non-eternal quality of ākāśa

definitions.definition: Sound has a beginning and is sense-perceived, hence non-eternal (NS 2.2.13ff.).

Sound is the mark of ākāśa, produced by conjunction, disjunction and sound (VS 2.1.24–27, 2.2.36–37 C); it is inarticulate or phonemic (Tarkasaṅgraha); later authors explain its travel to the ear on the model of waves or of kadamba buds.

notes: The wave / kadamba-bud models are recalled from later manuals.

definitions.definition: Word-meaning is the individual, form and universal together (NS 2.2.68); the relation of word and meaning is conventional (NS 2.1.56–57; NBh).
Understanding meaning from words is conventional (VS 7.2.24 C).
The denotative power is the Lord's convention (Tarkasaṅgraha); analysed in detail in the Śaktivāda and Śabdaśaktiprakāśikā.
Verbal cognition requires expectancy, compatibility, proximity and knowledge of intention (Tattvacintāmaṇi; Tarkasaṅgraha).

name: The Veda as authored by a reliable speaker

definitions.definition: The Veda is valid like mantra and medicine because its seers and teachers are reliable (NS 2.1.69; NBh); its validity rests on its being rooted in the Lord's perception (Gaṅgeśa); all Vedic sentences are valid because spoken by the Lord (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The composition of sentences in the Veda is preceded by understanding (VS 6.1.1 C); its authority follows from its being 'the statement of that' (VS 1.1.3).

A distinct self with qualities — free of demerit, false knowledge and heedlessness; with merit, knowledge and concentration; with eightfold lordship — who assists human effort and makes it fruitful, sets karma and the elements in motion, is like a reliable person and a father to beings (NS 4.1.19–21; NBh 4.1.21); the all-knowing maker proved by inference (NK 5.1; Gaṅgeśa); worshipped by all schools under different names (NK stabaka 1).
Maheśvara, by whose will creation and dissolution occur; saluted as the cause at the start of the Padārthadharmasaṅgraha. The Vaiśeṣika Sūtra itself does not name Īśvara.
The one omniscient supreme self with eternal cognition, desire and effort, author of the Veda, whose will fixes word-meanings (Tarkasaṅgraha).

relations.note: Yoga's Īśvara is a special puruṣa who is not the maker of the world; Nyāya's Īśvara is the efficient cause.

name: Udayana's proofs of Īśvara (NK 5.1)

definitions.definition: The all-knowing maker is proved from: (1) the world's being an effect (kārya); (2) the combining of atoms at creation (āyojana); (3) the support of the world (dhṛti) and (4) its destruction ('ādi'); (5) traditional skills and usage of words (pada); (6) the validity of the Veda (pratyaya); (7) scripture (śruti); (8) the Veda's consisting of sentences (vākya); (9) special number — the magnitude of dyads, which requires an enumerating cognition at creation (saṃkhyāviśeṣa). The five clusters first answer five objections.

notes: Counted as eight or nine depending on whether 'ādi' is taken separately; glosses follow the usual explanation.

definitions.definition: The invariable concomitance of probans with probandum ('wherever smoke, there fire'), known through observation of co-presence and absence of deviation, aided by tarka and extraordinary contact through the universal; defined exactly after rejecting five provisional definitions.

name: The five provisional definitions of pervasion (Vyāptipañcaka)

definitions.definition: Five definitions of pervasion in terms of non-occurrence in loci of the probandum's absence, each rejected chiefly because it fails for a probandum present everywhere (kevalānvayin).

name: Consideration (parāmarśa) as the instrument of inference

definitions.definition: The cognition 'this has smoke pervaded by fire' is the proximate cause of inferential cognition, not the memory of pervasion alone (Gaṅgeśa; Tarkasaṅgraha).
Absence of certainty not accompanied by a desire to infer.

name: The Navya-Nyāya analysis of cognition and its contents

definitions.definition: Every qualified cognition has a qualificand (viśeṣya), a qualifier (prakāra) and a relation (saṃsarga), with corresponding properties (viśeṣyatā, prakāratā, saṃsargatā) that determine one another (nirūpaka / nirūpita); properties and absences are specified by their delimitors, counterpositives and relations; valid cognition is apprehending in X the property X has as qualifier.

The property or relation that fixes the scope of another property — e.g. the counterpositiveness of 'absence of pot' is delimited by potness and by the relation (conjunction) through which the pot is denied; central to exact definitions such as that of pervasion.
Contact through the universal (grasping all instances), through a cognition (the presented content of a prior cognition), and born of yoga.
Conjunction; inherence in the conjoined; inherence in what inheres in the conjoined; inherence; inherence in what inheres; qualifier–qualified relation (Uddyotakara; Tarkasaṅgraha).
Read by Vācaspati into NS 1.1.4 ('non-verbalizable' and 'determinate').
Indeterminate perception ('this is something') is inferred, not perceived; determinate perception has a qualifier (Tarkasaṅgraha).

name: After-cognition (anuvyavasāya): cognition is known by a further cognition

definitions.definition: A cognition does not cognize itself; it is known by a subsequent inner perception 'I know this pot'.
The validity of a cognition is produced by excellences in its causes and known extrinsically — from the success of the activity it prompts (NBh 1.1.1) or other inference (Gaṅgeśa).
Error apprehends a property where it is absent (Tarkasaṅgraha; Gaṅgeśa).
False cognition is destroyed by knowledge of truth, as dream-notions on waking; it has a real substrate (NS 4.2.33–37).

name: New beginning (ārambha): the effect does not pre-exist

definitions.definition: The effect is not existent, non-existent-and-existent etc. before production, but is known to have been non-existent (NS 4.1.48–50); existence does not arise from non-existence (NS 4.1.14–18); an effect is the counterpositive of a prior absence (Tarkasaṅgraha).
Inherent (threads), non-inherent (their conjunction), efficient (loom); the instrument is the special cause (Tarkasaṅgraha).

name: Causal efficacy without a separate power (śakti)

definitions.definition: An effect follows from the totality of causes including the absence of counteragents; no distinct causal power need be posited (Udayana; Gaṅgeśa) — an enduring thing produces effects successively as auxiliaries join it (AtV).

name: Yogic perception and seers' knowledge

definitions.definition: The self is perceived through a special conjunction of self and mind, as are other substances (VS 9.13–17 C); yogins in concentration and out of it perceive the subtle, hidden and distant (Praśastapāda); seers' knowledge and the vision of the perfected arise from merit (VS 9.28).
The perception of one engaged in yoga arises from samādhi (NBh 1.1.3).

notes: The root texts give no warnings about such powers comparable to YS 3.37; none are recorded here.

definitions.definition: Knowledge: perception, inference, memory, seers' knowledge; non-knowledge: doubt, error, indefinite cognition, dream (Praśastapāda); non-knowledge arises from defects of senses and impressions (VS 9.25–27 C).
When the mind abides in the self (and does not join the senses), the embodied one has no pleasure or pain: that is yoga (VS 5.2.16–17 C).

relations.note: the Nyāya prescription of samādhi as the means to knowledge of truth
